Commandments
kuh-MAND-munts
noun (plural)
Old French commandement and Latin commandamentum — an authoritative order or precept; in biblical usage translates Hebrew mitzvot (מצות), the plural of mitzvah (מצוה), a divine commandment or obligation. The specific phrase “the commandments” most often refers to the Decalogue — the Aseret ha-Dibrot (“Ten Words” or “Ten Sayings”) given at Sinai. In the New Testament the Greek entolai (ἐντολαί) covers the same semantic ground, with Christ both summarizing the Law in two great commandments and extending its moral demand to the heart.

Biblical Definition

The commandments of God in Scripture span from the creational mandate of Genesis to the apostolic instructions of the epistles, but the word most centrally denotes the Decalogue — the Ten Words spoken by God at Sinai and inscribed twice on stone tablets (Exod 20; Deut 5). God prefaces the Decalogue with the covenant declaration: “I am the LORD thy God, which have brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage.” (Exod 20:2) — grounding every commandment in grace already given, not in merit to be earned. The Ten Commandments are not a ladder of works-righteousness but a covenant charter defining the life of a redeemed people.

Reformed theology divides the law into three uses: civil (restraining lawlessness in society), pedagogical (revealing sin and driving to Christ), and didactic or normative (guiding the regenerate life). The moral law summarized in the Decalogue remains binding upon believers as the standard of love toward God and neighbor (1689 LBCF 19.5). Christ Himself summarized the whole law in two commandments (Matt 22:37–40) and declared that love for Him is expressed through obedience: “If ye love me, keep my commandments.” (John 14:15).

The Shema — “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD:” (Deut 6:4) — stands as the theological foundation on which all commandment-keeping rests: monotheism precedes morality. The commandments are not arbitrary religious rules but the revealed character of the one God who redeems, and keeping them is the evidence of covenant faith.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines commandment as a mandate or order from superior authority; specifically in Scripture, one of the ten precepts given by God to Moses and recorded in Exodus 20, which are the foundation of the moral law and of all civil and religious duty.

COMMANDMENT, n. A command; a mandate; an order or injunction given by authority; charge; precept.

In Scripture, the ten commandments — the moral law given by God to Moses on Sinai — summarized first in the prohibition of other gods and graven images, then in obligations of worship, Sabbath, family, life, chastity, property, truth, and contentment.

COMMANDMENT in the New Testament sense includes all Christ's moral precepts and apostolic instructions, grounded in love: Christ reduced the whole law to love toward God with all the heart and love toward neighbor as oneself, declaring these the two great commandments on which all else hangs (Matt 22:37–40).

Key Scripture

Exod 20:2 — "I am the LORD thy God, which have brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage."

Exod 20:3 — "Thou shalt have no other gods before me."

Deut 6:4 — "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD:"

John 14:15 — "If ye love me, keep my commandments."

Modern Corruption

Modern antinomianism treats the commandments as obsolete covenant furniture the New Testament has dismantled; therapeutic culture replaces moral obligation with personal authenticity, making the self the only binding authority.

expand to see more

The oldest and most persistent corruption of the commandments is antinomianism — the claim that grace abolishes law so that the believer in Christ has no binding obligation to the moral precepts of God. Reformer-era antinomians (Johannes Agricola) and their modern descendants in hyper-grace preaching (Joseph Prince, Andrew Wommack) drive a wedge between gospel and law that neither Christ nor Paul permits. Christ came not to abolish the law but to fulfill it (Matt 5:17), and Paul insists that the gospel “establishes” rather than nullifies the law (Rom 3:31). The 1689 LBCF (19.5) explicitly confesses that the moral law contained in the Ten Commandments continues to bind all people, believers included, as the standard of righteous living.

A second corruption is the therapeutic reframing of the commandments as “guidelines for flourishing” rather than binding obligations from the sovereign God. This soft-pedaling replaces the divine imperative with a therapeutic invitation, as if the Decalogue were the Creator's suggestion for optimal life-management. The commandments are not advice; they are the word of the Lord who brought His people out of bondage. To obey them is to honor the God of the covenant; to disobey them is sin that requires the atonement Christ provided — not a suboptimal life-choice that requires therapeutic recalibration.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Rooted in the covenant economy of Sinai, the commandments carry the grammar of grace-before-law: God redeems first, then gives the charter of covenant life; the moral law flows from who God is, not from contractual negotiation.

expand to see more

Hebrew mitzvah / mitzvot (מצוה / מצות) — commandment, obligation; derived from tzivvah (to command); the plural mitzvot in rabbinic usage came to enumerate 613 total commandments in the Torah, of which the Decalogue is the foundational core

Hebrew Aseret ha-Dibrot — the Ten Words or Ten Sayings; the precise Hebrew name for the Decalogue, emphasizing that these are divine speech-acts, not merely written statutes, spoken directly by God before the people at Sinai (Exod 20:1)

Greek entolē (ἐντολή) — commandment, precept, injunction; used by Christ in John 14:15 and by Paul throughout his ethical sections to denote the ongoing moral obligations binding upon the redeemed life

The Shema (Deut 6:4) — “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one” — the theological premise on which all commandments rest; monotheism prior to morality; the God who commands is One, undivided, all-sovereign

The Reformation catechetical tradition — Luther's Large and Small Catechism, the Westminster Shorter Catechism, and the Baptist catechisms all open with the Decalogue as the first instructional unit, establishing the moral law as the foundation of Christian education

Usage

"The Westminster Shorter Catechism (Q&A 41–81) devotes forty questions to expounding the Ten Commandments, demonstrating that the Decalogue covers the whole range of human duty — worship, family, life, property, truth, and desire — and that each commandment forbids what it does not command and commands what it does not forbid."

"The Puritan tradition, following Calvin's Institutes (2.8), insisted that the commandments must be understood “expansively” — the prohibition of murder encompasses hatred; the prohibition of adultery encompasses lust; the positive command to love encompasses active service of the neighbor's good in every sphere."

"John's Gospel grounds the new covenant ethic explicitly in commandment-keeping: “If ye love me, keep my commandments.” (John 14:15); “If you keep My commandments, you will abide in My love, just as I have kept My Father's commandments and abide in His love” (John 15:10) — making obedience the evidence of genuine love, not an optional supplement to it."
